1020	# The CLI
1021	
1022	A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
1023	people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
1024	is plain HTTP, described in the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md); you never need the CLI.
1025	
1026	## Install
1027	
1028	macOS and Linux:
1029	
1030	```sh
1031	export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
1032	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh
1033	```
1034	
1035	Windows, in PowerShell (5.1 or 7):
1036	
1037	```powershell
1038	$env:ATIRA_API = "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai"
1039	irm "$env:ATIRA_API/install.ps1" | iex
1040	```
1041	
1042	The script checks for Node 24 or newer. Where it is missing, it asks whether to install a private copy for atira
1043	alone, the latest Node 24 from nodejs.org, checked against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt`. It needs no admin rights
1044	and never changes the `node` on your `PATH`. Without a terminal to ask in, `ATIRA_INSTALL_NODE=1` says yes (`0`, no).
1045	Then it downloads `/cli.mjs`, checks it against `/cli.mjs.sha256` and installs it for you alone, without sudo:
1046	
1047	- macOS and Linux: the file in `~/.local/share/atira/atira.mjs`, Node (if needed) in `~/.local/share/atira/node`,
1048	  and an `atira` command in `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`.
1049	- Windows: the same under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira`, with `atira.cmd` in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira\bin`, which it adds to
1050	  your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards.
1051	
1052	The `atira` command runs your own Node when it is 24 or newer, else the private copy. Running the installer again
1053	updates the CLI; it downloads Node again only when the private copy is older than 24. Read the script first, if you
1054	like:
1055	
1056	```sh
1057	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
1058	```
1059	
1060	To uninstall: `rm -rf ~/.local/share/atira ~/.local/bin/atira`, or on Windows
1061	`Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\atira"`. Your sign-in stays in the config file (see below) until you
1062	delete it.
1063	
1064	Without installing anything, download the file and run it with Node; `node atira.mjs` works wherever this guide
1065	says `atira`:
1066	
1067	```sh
1068	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
1069	```
1070	
1071	The CLI talks to the server it was downloaded from. Set `ATIRA_API` to use another one. `atira upgrade` downloads the
1072	server's current version, checks its SHA-256 and replaces the file; a download that does not match leaves the file
1073	as it was.
1074	
1075	## Sign in
1076	
1077	```sh
1078	atira login
1079	```
1080	
1081	The browser opens a page that asks you to sign in with GitHub, then whether to sign in the CLI on this computer.
1082	Approve, and the browser returns to the CLI, which stores a personal token for you. The token acts as you, on the
1083	team you are in at the time of each request: leave the team, or be removed, and it no longer reaches the team. It
1084	lasts 90 days. Your team page lists your signed-in devices; revoke any of them there.
1085	
1086	Where no browser can open (an SSH session, a container, a coding agent), sign in with a code instead:
1087	
1088	```sh
1089	atira login --device
1090	```
1091	
1092	It prints a link with the code filled in. Open it on any device, check that the code matches and approve; the CLI
1093	waits and then stores the token. `atira login` switches to the code by itself when the browser cannot be opened, or
1094	offers it when the browser has not answered after two minutes.
1095	
1096	```sh
1097	atira whoami                                  # who you are, your team, and when the token expires
1098	atira token                                   # the token, for curl and scripts
1099	curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" "$ATIRA_API/v1/teams/me"
1100	atira logout                                  # revoke the token on the server and forget it here
1101	```
1102	
1103	The token is kept per server in `~/.config/atira/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atira/config.json`; on Windows
1104	`%USERPROFILE%\.config\atira\config.json`), readable only by you (mode 0600). `ATIRA_TOKEN` overrides it, which suits
1105	CI and agents: `export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)`.
1106	
1107	## Commands
1108	
1109	| Command | What it does |
1110	| --- | --- |
1111	| `login [--device] [--key <key>]` | Sign in through the browser, or with a code (`--device`), and store a personal token; `--key` stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in |
1112	| `logout` | Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it |
1113	| `whoami` | Who you are signed in as, your team, and when the token expires |
1114	| `token` | Print the token in use, for `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)"` |
1115	| `upgrade` | Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file |
1116	| `challenges` | The challenges, with their Markdown pages |
1117	| `challenge <id>` | A challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema |
1118	| `scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]` | The published scouting logins for the public websites; `--env` prints them as shell exports for running your agent locally, with any hosted model's variables pointed at `atira models proxy`; use the same `--port` when the proxy runs on another port |
1119	| `models proxy [--port <port>]` | Where the organizers host models: a local proxy to them on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) that prints each model's base URL and key variables |
1120	| `test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset and open its run page; `--follow` prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here |
1121	| `submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder and submit it: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page; `--follow` prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here |
1122	| `cancel <run>` | Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails |
1123	| `final [--best-of <1\|3>] [--challenge <id>]` | Read or change the final attempt choice before the final run starts |
1124	| `status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]` | Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (`sub_...`), test run (`reh_...`) or run (`run_...`) |
1125	| `logs <run> [--follow]` | A test or scored run's logs; `--follow` keeps polling until the run has ended |
1126	| `package <id> [--out <dir>]` | The package a test run (`reh_...` or `run_...`), scored run or submission (`sub_...`) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; `--out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder, checked against its SHA-256 |
1127	| `leaderboard [--challenge <id>]` | The leaderboard |
1128	| `mcp` | Serve MCP on stdio for your coding agent: list and debug runs (why one failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared), start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm ([MCP guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)) |
1129	
1130	Every command accepts `--json` (machine-readable output on stdout, errors included) and `--help`.
1131	`--challenge` defaults to `ATIRA_CHALLENGE`, else the platform's first challenge. While `login` waits, it writes its
1132	instructions to stderr, so `--json` output on stdout stays one JSON document.
1133	
1134	### Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
1135	
1136	Develop against the public websites on your own machine, then test the package in the sandbox:
1137	
1138	```sh
1139	atira scout                    # the scouting logins: each website, its URL, username and password
1140	eval "$(atira scout --env)"    # the same as shell exports
1141	uv run python agent.py         # your agent, on your machine, against the public websites (the starter kit's way)
1142	atira test-run ./my-agent      # then one run in the sandbox, opened live in the browser
1143	```
1144	
1145	On Windows, `--env` and `models proxy` print PowerShell's `$env:NAME = '...'` instead; load them with
1146	`atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`.
1147	
1148	### Hosted models from your machine
1149	
1150	Where the organizers host models, a run gets each one's base URL and key variables set for it, and the
1151	Getting started page names them. On your machine, run the proxy in its own terminal: it prints the same variables,
1152	pointed at itself, with `local` as the key (any non-empty value works through it).
1153	
1154	```sh
1155	atira login                    # once per computer
1156	atira models proxy             # keep it running; it prints the exports
1157	```
1158	
1159	`eval "$(atira scout --env)"` sets the same variables with the scouting logins; it never exports your sign-in. The proxy
1160	listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It holds a 30-minute inference token, good for model calls only and bound to an Ed25519 key
1161	that never leaves the process, signs every call with that key and rotates the token before it expires. A copied token
1162	works in no other client. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. If port 8765 is in use, pick
1163	the same port for the proxy and the scouting exports:
1164	
1165	```sh
1166	atira models proxy --port 8777                   # in a second terminal
1167	eval "$(atira scout --env --port 8777)"
1168	```
1169	
1170	In PowerShell, the second line is `atira scout --env --port 8777 | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`. The proxy also
1171	prints the command with its actual port, including when `--port 0` lets the operating system choose one.
1172	
1173	`scout` needs no sign-in for the logins. It prints the logins the organizers published, how long they are valid,
1174	and what happens to an answer: these are demo logins, so an answer entered on the website that takes it is
1175	acknowledged without counting. For RFQ, a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting. `--json` prints what
1176	`GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returns: the logins as `access`, plus `submission`, `brief` and `answer_schema`,
1177	shaped like a run's `/v1/runs/current`. `--env` prints:
1178	
1179	| Variable | Value |
1180	| --- | --- |
1181	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | what `GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returned, as JSON: the brief, logins and answer format |
1182	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` | `$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/<id>/scouting`, the same without a token once the organizers publish the logins |
1183	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with the scouting logins, the JSON a run gets: `[{"siteId", "url", "credentials": {"username", "password"}}]` |
1184	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL` | each website's URL, its id upper-cased with `_` for other characters, e.g. `CHALLENGE_SITE_TENDER_PORTAL_URL` |
1185	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | only when the platform hosts models: each one through `atira models proxy` on this computer, with `local` as the key. Keep the proxy running in another terminal, signed in with `atira login`. `atira scout --help` names them |
1186	
1187	With `--env --json`, the same variables come as one JSON object. There is no run token: your agent calls other
1188	models with your own key, directly or through the model proxy with your personal token (see
1189	[LLM calls](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)). Calls through the proxy from your machine, a hosted model's included, are
1190	recorded for your team and never ranked. A hosted model is free to use, never charged; each call counts toward your
1191	run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest. Nothing done with these logins counts.
1192	Locally there are no browsers from the platform (`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `DISPLAY`) and no egress
1193	proxy: your agent starts its own browsers. When nothing is published yet, `scout` exits 4: organizers publish the scouting logins before the event.

1195	### Test runs and submissions
1196	
1197	```sh
1198	atira test-run ./my-agent --dry-run   # what would be uploaded, and what is left out
1199	atira test-run ./my-agent             # one run in the sandbox on the public dataset; opens its run page
1200	atira test-run ./my-agent --follow    # the same, and its logs here until it ends
1201	atira cancel run_...                  # stop a run that has not finished
1202	atira submit ./my-agent               # review, then the scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page
1203	atira status sub_...
1204	```
1205	
1206	`test-run` uploads the package, starts the test run and, when its output goes to a terminal, opens the run page in
1207	the browser: the browser, the logs, the phases and the score with its full breakdown, live. `submit` opens your team
1208	page instead, which shows the submission's review and then links each scored run as it starts: the run does not
1209	exist until the review has passed, which takes minutes, so the CLI does not wait for it unless you pass `--follow`.
1210	`ATIRA_BROWSER` picks the
1211	command that opens the page (`none` only prints the link), `--no-open` skips it, and `--json` never opens anything.
1212	
1213	`test-run --follow` then streams the run's logs as `logs --follow` does and exits 7 if the run failed or timed out.
1214	While the run waits for a sandbox, it prints its place in the [fair queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue) on stderr whenever
1215	that changes ("Queued: 3 runs ahead of yours"). With `--json --follow`, the upload's result comes as one JSON line,
1216	then one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` line per chunk. `submit --follow` prints the review's outcome, then each scored
1217	run's place in the queue and its end, and exits 7 unless the submission completes; with `--json`, the final
1218	submission follows the upload's line.
1219	
1220	`cancel <run>` takes a run (`run_...`) or a test run (`reh_...`) of your team that has not finished. The run's sandbox
1221	is removed and the run fails with the error "Cancelled by @you"; a queued run is cancelled before it starts. Your
1222	team can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run leaves its submission not complete: the leaderboard
1223	ignores that submission, and you can submit again. A run that
1224	has already finished answers 409 (exit 6).
1225	
1226	`test-run` and `submit` pack the folder into a gzipped tarball the way the platform reads it:
1227	
1228	- `agent.json` must be at the folder's root, with `run` (and optionally `setup`) as arrays of strings.
1229	- `.git`, `node_modules` and `.DS_Store` are always left out, and so is whatever `.gitignore` files exclude (in the
1230	  folder and below: patterns, `*`, `?`, `**`, `[...]`, a leading `/`, a trailing `/` for folders, and `!` to
1231	  include again). Symbolic links are left out too.
1232	- The limits are checked before uploading: at most 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, 20 MB in total, and 20 MB
1233	  compressed (or what the server announces).
1234	
1235	### Logs, status and the leaderboard
1236	
1237	`package <id>` shows exactly what a run ran: the package's SHA-256 and label, its `agent.json` and every file with
1238	its size. A scored run ran its submission's package. `--out ./downloaded` also saves the `.tar.gz` there; unpack it
1239	with `tar -xzf <file> -C <folder>`.
1240	
1241	`logs <run>` prints what the run has written so far; `--follow` polls with a growing pause (1 s, up to 10 s) and
1242	exits when the run has ended. `--json` prints one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` object per line. `status` without an id
1243	shows your best result, your latest submissions and your latest test runs.

1283	# Answers and scoring
1284	
1285	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
1286	
1287	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
1288	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
1289	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
1290	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
1291	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
1292	
1293	## Per run
1294	
1295	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
1296	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
1297	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
1298	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
1299	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
1300	
1301	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
1302	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
1303	
1304	## Leaderboard
1305	
1306	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
1307	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
1308	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
1309	the run's own value.
1310	
1311	1. Eligible before ineligible.
1312	2. Higher quality.
1313	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
1314	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
1315	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
1316	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
1317	
1318	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
1319	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
1320	
1321	Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
1322	values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
1323	
1324	## Final run
1325	
1326	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
1327	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
1328	
1329	## Winners
1330	
1331	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
1332	
1333	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
1334	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
1335	3. The elegance of the system.
1336	
1337	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
1338	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
1339	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
1340	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
1341	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
1342	
1343	## RFQ scoring
1344	
1345	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
1346	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
1347	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
1348	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
1349	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
1350	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
1351	
1352	| Part (a bid) | Points |
1353	| --- | --- |
1354	| Decision | 5 |
1355	| Tender reference | 5 |
1356	| Discount percent | 5 |
1357	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
1358	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
1359	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
1360	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
1361	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
1362	
1363	
1364	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
1365	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
1366	
1367	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
1368	one position's share each.
1369	
1370	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
1371	
1372	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
1373	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
1374	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
1375	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
1376	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
1377	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
1378	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
1379	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
1380	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
1381	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
1382	
1383	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
1384	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
1385	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

1391	# How a run works
1392	
1393	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
1394	
1395	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
1396	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
1397	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
1398	logins.
1399	
1400	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
1401	
1402	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
1403	
1404	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
1405	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
1406	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
1407	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
1408	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
1409	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
1410	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
1411	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
1412	   provider takes your own key.
1413	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
1414	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
1415	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
1416	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
1417	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
1418	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
1419	
1420	## Inside a run
1421	
1422	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
1423	   returns:
1424	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
1425	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
1426	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
1427	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
1428	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
1429	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
1430	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
1431	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
1432	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
1433	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
1434	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
1435	   provider's with your own key (below).
1436	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
1437	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
1438	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
1439	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
1440	     it again.
1441	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
1442	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
1443	
1444	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
1445	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
1446	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
1447	
1448	## LLM calls
1449	
1450	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
1451	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
1452	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
1453	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
1454	
1455	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
1456	
1457	```
1458	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
1459	```
1460	
1461	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
1462	
1463	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
1464	| --- | --- | --- |
1465	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
1466	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
1467	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
1468	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
1469	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
1470	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
1471	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
1472	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
1473	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
1474	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
1475	
1476	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
1477	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
1478	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
1479	
1480	### Your key
1481	
1482	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
1483	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
1484	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
1485	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
1486	
1487	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
1488	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
1489	as `x-api-key`:
1490	
1491	```python
1492	from openai import OpenAI
1493	
1494	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
1495	```
1496	
1497	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
1498	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
1499	
1500	```python
1501	import os
1502	from google import genai
1503	
1504	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
1505	    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
1506	```
1507	
1508	```javascript
1509	import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
1510	
1511	const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
1512	  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
1513	```
1514	
1515	A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
1516	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
1517	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
1518	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
1519	
1520	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
1521	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
1522	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
1523	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
1524	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
1525	`401`.
1526	
1527	A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
1528	context.
1529	
1530	### How cost is measured
1531	
1532	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
1533	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
1534	An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
1535	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
1536	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
1537	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
1538	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
1539	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
1540	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
1541	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
1542	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
1543	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
1544	
1545	The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
1546	charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
1547	
1548	### Team secrets
1549	
1550	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
1551	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
1552	
1553	```sh
1554	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
1555	  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
1556	curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
1557	curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
1558	```
1559	
1560	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
1561	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
1562	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
1563	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
1564	
1565	## Scored run
1566	
1567	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
1568	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
1569	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
1570	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
1571	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
1572	
1573	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
1574	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
1575	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
1576	  and the websites.
1577	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
1578	
1579	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
1580	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
1581	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
1582	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
1583	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
1584	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
1585	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
1586	   right after setup:
1587	
1588	   ```json
1589	   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
1590	   ```
1591	
1592	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
1593	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
1594	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
1595	
1596	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.

1598	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run

# Participant guide

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents. Eligible answers
rank first, then by how right they are, then by LLM cost times run time: halving either counts the same. New here?
`$API/start` walks you from sign-in to your first scored run, step by step.

- **Sign in and form a team:** sign in with GitHub at `$API/team`, create your team (you become its captain) and
  invite up to four teammates by their GitHub username (five people in all); each invite link works only for that
  account. Your team page shows members, rank and history.
- **Your terminal and your agent:** `curl -fsSL $API/install.sh | sh` (on Windows, in PowerShell:
  `irm $API/install.ps1 | iex`) installs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md), with a private Node 24 if yours is missing, and
  `atira login` signs it in through the browser. Each person gets their own token for each device, listed on the
  team page under Signed-in devices, where you can revoke it; `atira token` prints it for curl and scripts.
- **Everything in the browser:** your dashboard (`$API/team`) takes package uploads by drag and drop, lists every
  run with a link to its live view, and keeps your team's secrets.
- **Challenges:** each challenge is its own world with its own websites, task and answer format. The first one
  is [RFQ](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): turn a tender scattered across four German business websites into
  one priced bid.
- **Public and private data:** the websites and the scenario you scout and test-run on are the public dataset, and
  every scored submission runs on it during the hackathon. The correct answer isn't published; your system has to
  work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that
  passed review once by default, or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts, on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the winners
  ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from
  the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
- **Develop locally:** the scouting logins the organizers publish open the public websites to you and your agent.
  `atira scout --env` exports them the way a run gets its logins, so your agent runs on your machine against the
  real websites. Where the platform hosts models, they need no key there either: keep `atira models proxy` running
  and `--env` points your agent at it; any other provider takes your own key. Nothing done with them counts. RFQ has one public
  scenario, `public-1`.
- **Sandbox test runs:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live. It
  runs once in exactly the sandbox scored runs use, against the public scenario: watch its browser, read its logs,
  replay the recorded video, and get your score with the full breakdown. Use it to make sure your package works
  before you submit; `atira cancel` stops a run early.
- **Scored runs:** upload your agent system as a package. We review it, then run it once in the sandbox on the
  public dataset and score it. Only these runs count for the leaderboard. Your best submission holds your place on
  the leaderboard; your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
- **What wins:** eligible answers rank first, then answer quality; at equal quality, the lower LLM cost × wall-clock
  time wins, each measured on the submission's scored run. The final run ranks the same way, choosing your single best attempt if you opted in to three. Each public submission runs
  once.

| [How a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md) | before writing any code |
| [Building your agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/building-an-agent.md) | while building |
| [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md) | before your first test run |

The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton to start from (the plumbing, not an agent):
`mkdir my-agent && curl -fsSL $API/starter-kit.tar.gz | tar xz -C my-agent`.

Coding agents can help you: `$API/llms.txt` lists everything they need; the home page, Getting started, each

# The CLI

A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
is plain HTTP, described in the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md); you never need the CLI.

## Install

macOS and Linux:

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh
```

Windows, in PowerShell (5.1 or 7):

```powershell
$env:ATIRA_API = "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai"
irm "$env:ATIRA_API/install.ps1" | iex
```

The script checks for Node 24 or newer. Where it is missing, it asks whether to install a private copy for atira
alone, the latest Node 24 from nodejs.org, checked against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt`. It needs no admin rights
and never changes the `node` on your `PATH`. Without a terminal to ask in, `ATIRA_INSTALL_NODE=1` says yes (`0`, no).
Then it downloads `/cli.mjs`, checks it against `/cli.mjs.sha256` and installs it for you alone, without sudo:

- macOS and Linux: the file in `~/.local/share/atira/atira.mjs`, Node (if needed) in `~/.local/share/atira/node`,
  and an `atira` command in `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`.
- Windows: the same under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira`, with `atira.cmd` in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira\bin`, which it adds to
  your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards.

The `atira` command runs your own Node when it is 24 or newer, else the private copy. Running the installer again
updates the CLI; it downloads Node again only when the private copy is older than 24. Read the script first, if you
like:

```sh
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
```

To uninstall: `rm -rf ~/.local/share/atira ~/.local/bin/atira`, or on Windows
`Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\atira"`. Your sign-in stays in the config file (see below) until you
delete it.

Without installing anything, download the file and run it with Node; `node atira.mjs` works wherever this guide
says `atira`:

```sh
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
```

The CLI talks to the server it was downloaded from. Set `ATIRA_API` to use another one. `atira upgrade` downloads the
server's current version, checks its SHA-256 and replaces the file; a download that does not match leaves the file
as it was.

## Sign in

```sh
atira login
```

The browser opens a page that asks you to sign in with GitHub, then whether to sign in the CLI on this computer.
Approve, and the browser returns to the CLI, which stores a personal token for you. The token acts as you, on the
team you are in at the time of each request: leave the team, or be removed, and it no longer reaches the team. It
lasts 90 days. Your team page lists your signed-in devices; revoke any of them there.

Where no browser can open (an SSH session, a container, a coding agent), sign in with a code instead:

```sh
atira login --device
```

It prints a link with the code filled in. Open it on any device, check that the code matches and approve; the CLI
waits and then stores the token. `atira login` switches to the code by itself when the browser cannot be opened, or
offers it when the browser has not answered after two minutes.

```sh
atira whoami                                  # who you are, your team, and when the token expires
atira token                                   # the token, for curl and scripts
curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" "$ATIRA_API/v1/teams/me"
atira logout                                  # revoke the token on the server and forget it here
```

The token is kept per server in `~/.config/atira/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atira/config.json`; on Windows
`%USERPROFILE%\.config\atira\config.json`), readable only by you (mode 0600). `ATIRA_TOKEN` overrides it, which suits
CI and agents: `export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)`.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `login [--device] [--key <key>]` | Sign in through the browser, or with a code (`--device`), and store a personal token; `--key` stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in |
| `logout` | Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it |
| `whoami` | Who you are signed in as, your team, and when the token expires |
| `token` | Print the token in use, for `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)"` |
| `upgrade` | Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file |
| `challenges` | The challenges, with their Markdown pages |
| `challenge <id>` | A challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema |
| `scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]` | The published scouting logins for the public websites; `--env` prints them as shell exports for running your agent locally, with any hosted model's variables pointed at `atira models proxy`; use the same `--port` when the proxy runs on another port |
| `models proxy [--port <port>]` | Where the organizers host models: a local proxy to them on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) that prints each model's base URL and key variables |
| `test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset and open its run page; `--follow` prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here |
| `submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder and submit it: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page; `--follow` prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here |
| `cancel <run>` | Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails |
| `final [--best-of <1\|3>] [--challenge <id>]` | Read or change the final attempt choice before the final run starts |
| `status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]` | Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (`sub_...`), test run (`reh_...`) or run (`run_...`) |
| `logs <run> [--follow]` | A test or scored run's logs; `--follow` keeps polling until the run has ended |
| `package <id> [--out <dir>]` | The package a test run (`reh_...` or `run_...`), scored run or submission (`sub_...`) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; `--out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder, checked against its SHA-256 |
| `leaderboard [--challenge <id>]` | The leaderboard |
| `mcp` | Serve MCP on stdio for your coding agent: list and debug runs (why one failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared), start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm ([MCP guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)) |

Every command accepts `--json` (machine-readable output on stdout, errors included) and `--help`.
`--challenge` defaults to `ATIRA_CHALLENGE`, else the platform's first challenge. While `login` waits, it writes its
instructions to stderr, so `--json` output on stdout stays one JSON document.

### Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

Develop against the public websites on your own machine, then test the package in the sandbox:

```sh
atira scout                    # the scouting logins: each website, its URL, username and password
eval "$(atira scout --env)"    # the same as shell exports
uv run python agent.py         # your agent, on your machine, against the public websites (the starter kit's way)
atira test-run ./my-agent      # then one run in the sandbox, opened live in the browser
```

On Windows, `--env` and `models proxy` print PowerShell's `$env:NAME = '...'` instead; load them with
`atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`.

### Hosted models from your machine

Where the organizers host models, a run gets each one's base URL and key variables set for it, and the
Getting started page names them. On your machine, run the proxy in its own terminal: it prints the same variables,
pointed at itself, with `local` as the key (any non-empty value works through it).

```sh
atira login                    # once per computer
atira models proxy             # keep it running; it prints the exports
```

`eval "$(atira scout --env)"` sets the same variables with the scouting logins; it never exports your sign-in. The proxy
listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It holds a 30-minute inference token, good for model calls only and bound to an Ed25519 key
that never leaves the process, signs every call with that key and rotates the token before it expires. A copied token
works in no other client. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. If port 8765 is in use, pick
the same port for the proxy and the scouting exports:

```sh
atira models proxy --port 8777                   # in a second terminal
eval "$(atira scout --env --port 8777)"
```

In PowerShell, the second line is `atira scout --env --port 8777 | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`. The proxy also
prints the command with its actual port, including when `--port 0` lets the operating system choose one.

`scout` needs no sign-in for the logins. It prints the logins the organizers published, how long they are valid,
and what happens to an answer: these are demo logins, so an answer entered on the website that takes it is
acknowledged without counting. For RFQ, a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting. `--json` prints what
`GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returns: the logins as `access`, plus `submission`, `brief` and `answer_schema`,
shaped like a run's `/v1/runs/current`. `--env` prints:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | what `GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returned, as JSON: the brief, logins and answer format |
| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` | `$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/<id>/scouting`, the same without a token once the organizers publish the logins |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with the scouting logins, the JSON a run gets: `[{"siteId", "url", "credentials": {"username", "password"}}]` |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL` | each website's URL, its id upper-cased with `_` for other characters, e.g. `CHALLENGE_SITE_TENDER_PORTAL_URL` |
| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | only when the platform hosts models: each one through `atira models proxy` on this computer, with `local` as the key. Keep the proxy running in another terminal, signed in with `atira login`. `atira scout --help` names them |

With `--env --json`, the same variables come as one JSON object. There is no run token: your agent calls other
models with your own key, directly or through the model proxy with your personal token (see
[LLM calls](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)). Calls through the proxy from your machine, a hosted model's included, are
recorded for your team and never ranked. A hosted model is free to use, never charged; each call counts toward your
run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest. Nothing done with these logins counts.
Locally there are no browsers from the platform (`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `DISPLAY`) and no egress
proxy: your agent starts its own browsers. When nothing is published yet, `scout` exits 4: organizers publish the scouting logins before the event.

### Test runs and submissions

```sh
atira test-run ./my-agent --dry-run   # what would be uploaded, and what is left out
atira test-run ./my-agent             # one run in the sandbox on the public dataset; opens its run page
atira test-run ./my-agent --follow    # the same, and its logs here until it ends
atira cancel run_...                  # stop a run that has not finished
atira submit ./my-agent               # review, then the scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page
atira status sub_...
```

`test-run` uploads the package, starts the test run and, when its output goes to a terminal, opens the run page in
the browser: the browser, the logs, the phases and the score with its full breakdown, live. `submit` opens your team
page instead, which shows the submission's review and then links each scored run as it starts: the run does not
exist until the review has passed, which takes minutes, so the CLI does not wait for it unless you pass `--follow`.
`ATIRA_BROWSER` picks the
command that opens the page (`none` only prints the link), `--no-open` skips it, and `--json` never opens anything.

`test-run --follow` then streams the run's logs as `logs --follow` does and exits 7 if the run failed or timed out.
While the run waits for a sandbox, it prints its place in the [fair queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue) on stderr whenever
that changes ("Queued: 3 runs ahead of yours"). With `--json --follow`, the upload's result comes as one JSON line,
then one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` line per chunk. `submit --follow` prints the review's outcome, then each scored
run's place in the queue and its end, and exits 7 unless the submission completes; with `--json`, the final
submission follows the upload's line.

`cancel <run>` takes a run (`run_...`) or a test run (`reh_...`) of your team that has not finished. The run's sandbox
is removed and the run fails with the error "Cancelled by @you"; a queued run is cancelled before it starts. Your
team can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run leaves its submission not complete: the leaderboard
ignores that submission, and you can submit again. A run that
has already finished answers 409 (exit 6).

`test-run` and `submit` pack the folder into a gzipped tarball the way the platform reads it:

- `agent.json` must be at the folder's root, with `run` (and optionally `setup`) as arrays of strings.
- `.git`, `node_modules` and `.DS_Store` are always left out, and so is whatever `.gitignore` files exclude (in the
  folder and below: patterns, `*`, `?`, `**`, `[...]`, a leading `/`, a trailing `/` for folders, and `!` to
  include again). Symbolic links are left out too.
- The limits are checked before uploading: at most 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, 20 MB in total, and 20 MB
  compressed (or what the server announces).

### Logs, status and the leaderboard

`package <id>` shows exactly what a run ran: the package's SHA-256 and label, its `agent.json` and every file with
its size. A scored run ran its submission's package. `--out ./downloaded` also saves the `.tar.gz` there; unpack it
with `tar -xzf <file> -C <folder>`.

`logs <run>` prints what the run has written so far; `--follow` polls with a growing pause (1 s, up to 10 s) and
exits when the run has ended. `--json` prints one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` object per line. `status` without an id
shows your best result, your latest submissions and your latest test runs.

## Configuration

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ATIRA_API` | The platform; defaults to the server the file came from |
| `ATIRA_TOKEN` | A token to use instead of the stored one |
| `ATIRA_CHALLENGE` | The default challenge |
| `ATIRA_POLL_MS` | The first pause of `logs --follow`, in milliseconds (default 1000) |
| `ATIRA_BROWSER` | The command `login`, `test-run` and `submit` open pages with, or `none` to only print the link |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Where `atira/config.json` lives (default `~/.config`) |

The config file holds `{"servers": {"<ATIRA_API>": {"token": "atp_...", "token_id", "expires_at", "login"}}}`.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Done |
| 1 | Network or server error |
| 2 | Usage: unknown command or option, a missing argument, a folder that does not exist |
| 3 | Not signed in, sign-in cancelled or expired, or the server refused the credential (401, 403) |
| 4 | Not found (404) |
| 5 | Invalid request or package: a missing `agent.json`, over a limit, a 400 or 413 |
| 6 | Busy: a submission already in evaluation, three test runs already waiting, a rate limit, or cancelling a finished run (409, 429) |
| 7 | `logs --follow` or `test-run --follow`: the run failed or timed out; `submit --follow`: the submission did not complete |

With `--json`, an error is printed as `{"error": {"code", "message", "status"}}` on stdout.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
page or with `atira final --best-of 3` before the final run starts. Your best attempt counts. Details:
[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).

# Answers and scoring

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).

## Per run

- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.

A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.

## Leaderboard

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
the run's own value.

1. Eligible before ineligible.
2. Higher quality.
3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.

On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
the teams no other eligible team beats on both.

Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.

## Final run

When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.

## Winners

We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:

1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
3. The elegance of the system.

It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).

## RFQ scoring

The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.

| Part (a bid) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | 5 |
| Tender reference | 5 |
| Discount percent | 5 |
| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |


For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
points but leaves the other fields their credit.

Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
one position's share each.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.

Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

### Team secrets

Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh
curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.

## Scored run

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
